topics.label: Introduction and learning objectives
topics.groupedBecause: This opening frames the lecture within the cancer course and states what students should learn.

topics.label: Genetic origins and evolution of cancer
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics explain how mutations arise and enable susceptible cells to evolve into cancer within a permissive environment.

topics.label: Environmental cancer risks and evidence for their contribution
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics examine the contribution of environmental exposure to cancer risk and how that contribution is inferred and interpreted.

topics.label: Infection-associated carcinogenesis
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics explain how infectious agents contribute to cancer, using Burkitt lymphoma as a detailed example.

topics.label: DNA damage mechanisms of environmental carcinogens
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics trace how environmental exposures produce DNA damage that can become cancer-driving mutations.

topics.label: Tumour initiation and promotion
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics distinguish mutation-producing initiation from the promotional conditions that allow initiated cells to proliferate into tumours.

topics.label: Biological context of carcinogen action
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics explain and recap how biological context determines whether exposure to a carcinogen contributes to cancer development.

topics.label: Human evidence linking carcinogen exposure to cancer
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics show how evidence collected from human populations and cancer genomes can link particular exposures to cancer.

topics.label: Experimental carcinogenicity testing and its limitations
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics examine controlled experimental tests of carcinogenic potential and why their results may not fully predict human cancer risk.

topics.label: Closing summary and risk–benefit decisions
topics.groupedBecause: This closing synthesises the lecture's conclusions around the risk–benefit decisions involved in carcinogen exposure.
